Gustave Flaubert was the French novelist who elevated realism into an obsessive aesthetic philosophy and established himself as a master of psychological insight and linguistic precision. Through works like Madame Bovary and Salammbô, he demonstrated that the mundane provincial life and internal monologue of ordinary people could be as artistically significant as historical epics or romantic adventure, fundamentally reshaping how literature understood itself.

Born in Rouen, the son of a doctor, his provincial petit-bourgeois childhood and family life became the template for his fictional explorations of provincial ennui and moral disappointment. Madame Bovary, published in eighteen fifty-six, is his masterpiece. It depicts an adulterous provincial wife's self-destructive romantic fantasies. Its realism and frank treatment of female sexuality scandalized France and led to his prosecution for immorality, though he was acquitted.

He pioneered the concept of style as moral and philosophical commitment. He believed perfect prose was a supreme good, rewrote passages obsessively, and believed an author should be everywhere present yet nowhere visible in the text. He spent years researching each novel, traveling to historical locations and amassing documentation. For Salammbô, he journeyed to Tunisia to faithfully recreate Carthage's material culture.

His famous dictum "Madame Bovary, c'est moi"—Madame Bovary is me—paradoxically asserts both the author's distance from their creation and the author's complete psychological investment in it. He mentored Guy de Maupassant, the great short-story writer, and influenced virtually every realist and naturalist writer after him, from the Russians to the American modernists.

He pioneered the technique of style indirect libre, or free indirect discourse, allowing readers access to characters' consciousness while maintaining narrative distance and irony. He struggled with poverty and depression throughout his career, particularly after Madame Bovary's success. The legal case surrounding its publication haunted him and reinforced his conviction that the artist must stand apart from society. His aesthetic principle of impassibilité—authorial detachment and objectivity—deliberately rejected Romantic emotionalism, forcing readers to draw their own moral judgments from unmoralized observation.
